contentHtml:
The whitepaper covers the key legal and regulatory updates impacting healthcare businesses, encompassing investment, operations, technology and risks

As the healthcare sector in India embraces data-driven care, artificial intelligence (AI) and digitally enabled delivery models, businesses must confront critical questions on patient-data governance, the clinical deployment of AI and heightened compliance obligations. Khaitan & Co and NATHEALTH’s joint whitepaper The Anatomy of India’s Healthcare Sector: Understanding the Legal and Regulatory Landscape released today throws light on key considerations and practical issues that have emerged as central to healthcare providers, health-tech companies and investors in the country.

Launched at NATHEALTH’s Governing Council and Western Region CXO Conclave in Mumbai, the whitepaper provides in-depth insights and covers important legal and regulatory developments within the healthcare sector.

Anand Mehta, Partner, Khaitan & Co said, “India’s healthcare sector is fast becoming a hub for innovation, as technology reshapes how care is accessed and delivered. But rising investment, consolidation and a wave of regulatory reform have brought new complexity, particularly around patient data and the clinical use of AI. Stakeholders who understand the legal and governance framework early will be best placed to grow responsibly and improve patient outcomes.”

Aditya Patni, Partner, Khaitan & Co, said, “How healthcare businesses raise capital, and the operating models they build, will shape their growth. With private equity and debt financing both playing a larger role, and many promoter-led hospital groups now confronting succession and consolidation, transactions demand closer attention to governance and to how risk is allocated between parties. Getting tax and regulatory structuring right early, well before diligence begins, is increasingly decisive. This whitepaper brings together our perspectives on the legal issues that drive investment decisions and business structures in Indian healthcare.”

Dr Sangita Reddy, President, NATHEALTH and Joint Managing Director, Apollo Hospitals, said “Healthcare can no longer begin and end with a hospital visit. It must progress from episodic treatment to a system that places holistic prevention at its core. That transition is already visible. Artificial intelligence and continuous health monitoring are enabling the early detection of risk, often long before illness takes hold. India must embrace this digital revolution with conviction and build devices and algorithms attuned to the needs and characteristics of Indian populations.”

Varun Khanna, Vice President, NATHEALTH and Managing Director & Group CEO, Aster DM Quality Care, said, “India’s healthcare sector is at an inflection point. Hospitals are growing, investment is required to create access, enhance technology investments to ensure benchmark clinical outcomes. That progress brings important questions: how patient data is protected, how AI is used responsibly in clinical decisions, and where accountability lies when technology supports care. Providers and investors need clear answers to these early, not after the fact. This whitepaper with Khaitan & Co sets out the legal and regulatory landscape in a practical way, from funding and succession planning to competition, environmental compliance and tax. It will help hospital leaders, boards and investors plan with confidence.”

The India Brand Equity Foundation (IBEF) estimates the hospital market in India to be worth USD 122.3 billion in 2025, and is projected to reach USD 202.5 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 10.61 per cent. Data from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare’s National Health Accounts Estimates for 2022–23 shows that government health expenditure increased threefold between 2013–14 and 2022–23, reaching Rs 3.85 lakh crore.

The whitepaper gives a discerning perspective for hospitals, healthcare operators, investors, health-tech businesses and other players across operational aspects, regulatory frameworks, technology advancements and a sectoral perspective. It further elaborates key legal and commercial developments in the ecosystem, from private funding, debt-financing and succession planning for hospitals, to the importance of competition and antitrust, environmental compliance, tax considerations and AI adoption.

Healthcare businesses have seen an uptick in investments as well as deeper technology integration and it is imperative to address questions around patient data, the clinical use of AI and liability in cases of technology-assisted decisions. AI-enabled diagnostics, clinical decision-support systems and telemedicine can potentially give a significant fillip to the sector while meaningfully extending access to care beyond traditional healthcare facilities. Investors too need to consider several regulatory factors such as tax and regulatory structuring at the pre-diligence stage, while the sector faces closer regulatory scrutiny alongside infrastructure, supply-chain and workforce challenges that call for greater oversight from management and boards.
